title: Plant Biochemistry
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L Plant Biochemistry curriculum: photosynthesis (light reactions, Calvin cycle, C3/C4/CAM pathways, photorespiration), plant cell wall composition, secondary metabolites, plant hormone biochemistry, nitrogen fixation and assimilation, plant pigments, and stress/defense biochemistry, building on 200-300L general and plant-related biochemistry.

questions.question: During the light reactions of photosynthesis, photosystem II oxidizes water primarily to:
options: Replace electrons lost from the reaction center chlorophyll (P680) after light excitation, releasing O2 and protons
Generate ATP directly without an electron transport chain
Reduce NADP+ to NADPH directly
Provide carbon skeletons for the Calvin cycle
questions.correct_answer: Replace electrons lost from the reaction center chlorophyll (P680) after light excitation, releasing O2 and protons
questions.explanation: The oxygen-evolving complex of photosystem II splits water to replace electrons donated by excited P680, releasing O2 as a byproduct and contributing protons to the thylakoid lumen for the proton gradient.

questions.question: The 'Z-scheme' of photosynthetic electron transport describes the sequential flow of electrons through which order of components?
options: Water to PSII to plastoquinone to cytochrome b6f to plastocyanin to PSI to ferredoxin to NADP+
NADPH to PSI to PSII to water
CO2 to RuBisCO to PSII directly
ATP synthase to PSI to PSII
questions.correct_answer: Water to PSII to plastoquinone to cytochrome b6f to plastocyanin to PSI to ferredoxin to NADP+
questions.explanation: The Z-scheme depicts the redox potential changes as electrons flow from water (low potential after oxidation input) through PSII, the plastoquinone pool, cytochrome b6f complex, plastocyanin, PSI, ferredoxin, and finally to NADP+ via ferredoxin-NADP+ reductase.

questions.question: Cyclic photophosphorylation differs from non-cyclic (linear) photophosphorylation in that it:
options: Generates ATP using only photosystem I, without producing NADPH or evolving O2
Uses only photosystem II and produces both ATP and NADPH
Requires no proton gradient
Occurs only in the stroma, not the thylakoid membrane
questions.correct_answer: Generates ATP using only photosystem I, without producing NADPH or evolving O2
questions.explanation: In cyclic photophosphorylation, electrons from excited PSI return to the cytochrome b6f complex and back to PSI instead of reducing NADP+, generating additional ATP to supplement the Calvin cycle's ATP:NADPH requirement without net O2 evolution.

questions.question: RuBisCO (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase) catalyzes the carboxylation of RuBP with CO2 to yield:
options: Two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate
One molecule of fructose-6-phosphate directly
Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and ATP
Oxaloacetate and phosphoenolpyruvate
questions.correct_answer: Two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate
questions.explanation: RuBisCO adds CO2 to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (a 5-carbon sugar), forming an unstable 6-carbon intermediate that immediately splits into two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA), the first stable product of the Calvin cycle.

questions.question: The Calvin cycle can be divided into three phases: carboxylation, reduction, and regeneration. The reduction phase requires:
options: ATP and NADPH to convert 3-phosphoglycerate to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate
Only ATP, with NADPH used solely in regeneration
Light directly acting on RuBisCO
CO2 fixation without any cofactors
questions.correct_answer: ATP and NADPH to convert 3-phosphoglycerate to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate
questions.explanation: 3-Phosphoglycerate is first phosphorylated by ATP to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, then reduced by NADPH (via glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase) to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, consuming both ATP and NADPH generated in the light reactions.

questions.question: RuBisCO's oxygenase activity, which competes with carboxylation and initiates photorespiration, produces which two products from RuBP and O2?
options: 3-phosphoglycerate and 2-phosphoglycolate
Two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate
Glycine and serine directly
Glyoxylate and glycerate
questions.correct_answer: 3-phosphoglycerate and 2-phosphoglycolate
questions.explanation: When RuBisCO acts as an oxygenase, O2 reacts with RuBP to yield one molecule of 3-phosphoglycerate and one molecule of 2-phosphoglycolate, the latter entering the photorespiratory pathway across chloroplasts, peroxisomes, and mitochondria.

questions.question: Photorespiration is considered metabolically wasteful for C3 plants mainly because it:
options: Consumes ATP and O2 while releasing previously fixed CO2, without net synthesis of carbohydrate
Produces more ATP than the Calvin cycle itself
Occurs only in darkness
Directly increases RuBisCO's affinity for CO2
questions.correct_answer: Consumes ATP and O2 while releasing previously fixed CO2, without net synthesis of carbohydrate
questions.explanation: Photorespiration salvages carbon from 2-phosphoglycolate but in doing so releases CO2 (in the mitochondrial glycine decarboxylase step) and consumes ATP and reducing power, resulting in a net energetic cost and loss of fixed carbon under high O2/low CO2 conditions.

questions.question: C4 plants such as maize and sugarcane minimize photorespiration by:
options: Spatially separating initial CO2 fixation (via PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells) from the Calvin cycle (in bundle sheath cells), concentrating CO2 around RuBisCO
Performing the entire Calvin cycle at night
Eliminating RuBisCO entirely
Using only photosystem I for carbon fixation
questions.correct_answer: Spatially separating initial CO2 fixation (via PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells) from the Calvin cycle (in bundle sheath cells), concentrating CO2 around RuBisCO
questions.explanation: In C4 photosynthesis, PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells fixes CO2 as HCO3- into oxaloacetate/malate (or aspartate), which is transported to bundle sheath cells and decarboxylated to release CO2 at high concentration around RuBisCO, suppressing its oxygenase activity.

questions.question: PEP carboxylase, the primary carboxylating enzyme in C4 and CAM plants, differs functionally from RuBisCO in that it:
options: Fixes bicarbonate (HCO3-) rather than CO2 directly and has no oxygenase activity
Also catalyzes an oxygenase reaction with O2
Is located exclusively in bundle sheath chloroplasts
Requires light for activation, unlike RuBisCO
questions.correct_answer: Fixes bicarbonate (HCO3-) rather than CO2 directly and has no oxygenase activity
questions.explanation: PEP carboxylase uses HCO3- (formed from CO2 by carbonic anhydrase) as substrate to carboxylate phosphoenolpyruvate to oxaloacetate, and unlike RuBisCO it does not react with O2, giving it no competing oxygenase reaction.

questions.question: CAM (Crassulacean Acid Metabolism) plants, adapted to arid environments, differ from C4 plants primarily in that they:
options: Temporally separate CO2 fixation (at night, stomata open) from the Calvin cycle (during the day, stomata closed), rather than spatially separating them
Lack PEP carboxylase entirely
Fix CO2 only during the day
Perform C4-type fixation without ever using RuBisCO
questions.correct_answer: Temporally separate CO2 fixation (at night, stomata open) from the Calvin cycle (during the day, stomata closed), rather than spatially separating them
questions.explanation: CAM plants (e.g. cacti, pineapple) open stomata at night to fix CO2 via PEP carboxylase into malate, stored in the vacuole; during the day, stomata close to minimize water loss while malate is decarboxylated to supply CO2 to RuBisCO for the light-dependent Calvin cycle.

questions.question: The primary structural polysaccharide of the plant primary cell wall, composed of beta-1,4-linked glucose units forming microfibrils, is:
options: Cellulose
Starch
Glycogen
Chitin
questions.correct_answer: Cellulose
questions.explanation: Cellulose consists of linear chains of beta-1,4-glucan that hydrogen-bond into crystalline microfibrils, providing the primary tensile strength of the plant cell wall, distinct from the alpha-1,4 linkages of storage starch.

questions.question: Hemicelluloses in the plant cell wall function mainly to:
options: Cross-link cellulose microfibrils, forming a cohesive network with the wall matrix
Serve as the main energy storage polysaccharide in seeds
Replace cellulose in secondary walls entirely
Act as the primary photosynthetic pigment carrier
questions.correct_answer: Cross-link cellulose microfibrils, forming a cohesive network with the wall matrix
questions.explanation: Hemicelluloses such as xyloglucans hydrogen-bond to the surface of cellulose microfibrils, tethering them together and integrating them into the broader wall matrix alongside pectins.

questions.question: Lignin, deposited mainly in secondary cell walls of vascular plants, is a complex polymer synthesized from:
options: Phenylpropanoid monomers (monolignols) such as coniferyl, sinapyl, and coumaryl alcohols
Glucose units linked by beta-1,4 bonds
Amino acids linked by peptide bonds
Fatty acid chains esterified to glycerol
questions.correct_answer: Phenylpropanoid monomers (monolignols) such as coniferyl, sinapyl, and coumaryl alcohols
questions.explanation: Lignin is formed by oxidative radical polymerization of monolignols derived from the phenylpropanoid pathway, producing a rigid, hydrophobic polymer that provides mechanical strength and resistance to microbial degradation in woody tissue.

questions.question: Pectins, abundant in the middle lamella and primary cell wall, are rich in which sugar acid that gives them their gel-forming property?
options: Galacturonic acid
Glucuronic acid only
Gluconic acid
Ascorbic acid
questions.correct_answer: Galacturonic acid
questions.explanation: Pectins are largely composed of polygalacturonic acid chains (homogalacturonan); the carboxyl groups on galacturonic acid can be cross-linked by Ca2+ ions ('egg-box' model), giving pectin its characteristic gel-forming ability important in cell adhesion.

questions.question: The enzyme nitrogenase, responsible for biological nitrogen fixation in root-nodule bacteria such as Rhizobium, converts atmospheric N2 into:
options: Ammonia (NH3), consuming large amounts of ATP and reducing equivalents
Nitrate (NO3-) directly
Nitrous oxide (N2O) as the primary product
Urea
questions.correct_answer: Ammonia (NH3), consuming large amounts of ATP and reducing equivalents
questions.explanation: Nitrogenase reduces N2 to NH3 in an energetically expensive reaction requiring roughly 16 ATP and 8 electrons per N2 molecule, and is extremely oxygen-sensitive, which is why leghemoglobin in nodules helps maintain a low free-O2 environment.

questions.question: Leghemoglobin in root nodules serves the important function of:
options: Binding and buffering free oxygen to protect the oxygen-labile nitrogenase enzyme while still allowing sufficient O2 for bacteroid respiration
Directly catalyzing the reduction of N2 to ammonia
Transporting fixed nitrogen to the xylem
Providing pigmentation for pollinator attraction
questions.correct_answer: Binding and buffering free oxygen to protect the oxygen-labile nitrogenase enzyme while still allowing sufficient O2 for bacteroid respiration
questions.explanation: Leghemoglobin, synthesized cooperatively by plant and bacterial genes, has a high affinity for O2, keeping free O2 concentrations very low to protect nitrogenase while still delivering enough O2 to support bacteroid oxidative respiration for ATP.

questions.question: In plants, ammonia produced by nitrogen fixation or nitrate reduction is assimilated into organic form mainly through the sequential action of:
options: Glutamine synthetase and glutamate synthase (the GS-GOGAT pathway)
Urease and arginase
Glutamate dehydrogenase acting alone at physiological ammonia concentrations
Nitrate reductase and nitrite reductase only
questions.correct_answer: Glutamine synthetase and glutamate synthase (the GS-GOGAT pathway)
questions.explanation: Glutamine synthetase incorporates NH3 into glutamate to form glutamine (using ATP), and glutamate synthase (GOGAT) then transfers the amide nitrogen of glutamine to 2-oxoglutarate, regenerating two glutamates; this GS-GOGAT cycle is the primary route of ammonia assimilation in plants at physiological concentrations.

questions.question: Nitrate reductase, the first enzyme in nitrate assimilation, reduces nitrate to nitrite using electrons from:
options: NADH (or NADPH in some species)
Ferredoxin directly in the cytosol
ATP hydrolysis
Molecular oxygen
questions.correct_answer: NADH (or NADPH in some species)
questions.explanation: Cytosolic nitrate reductase uses NADH (the more common electron donor in higher plants) to reduce NO3- to NO2-, which is then transported into the chloroplast where nitrite reductase, using reduced ferredoxin, further reduces it to NH3.

questions.question: Chlorophyll a and b differ structurally in that chlorophyll b has:
options: A formyl group (-CHO) at the C7 position of the porphyrin ring in place of chlorophyll a's methyl group (-CH3)
No magnesium in its porphyrin ring
An additional phytol tail
A carotenoid group attached directly to it
questions.correct_answer: A formyl group (-CHO) at the C7 position of the porphyrin ring in place of chlorophyll a's methyl group (-CH3)
questions.explanation: This small substituent difference shifts chlorophyll b's absorption spectrum slightly relative to chlorophyll a, broadening the range of light wavelengths a plant can capture and funnel toward the reaction center as an accessory pigment.

questions.question: Carotenoids in the photosynthetic apparatus serve two major functions:
options: Light-harvesting (accessory pigments) and photoprotection by quenching excess excitation energy and reactive oxygen species such as singlet oxygen
Direct catalysis of water splitting and only that function
Serving as the sole electron acceptor in photosystem I
Structural support of the thylakoid membrane only
questions.correct_answer: Light-harvesting (accessory pigments) and photoprotection by quenching excess excitation energy and reactive oxygen species such as singlet oxygen
questions.explanation: Carotenoids absorb light in the blue-green region (extending the light-harvesting range) and also dissipate excess absorbed energy as heat (non-photochemical quenching) and quench singlet oxygen and triplet chlorophyll, protecting the photosynthetic apparatus from photo-oxidative damage.

questions.question: Anthocyanins, water-soluble pigments responsible for red, purple, and blue coloration in many fruits and flowers, are chemically classified as:
options: Flavonoids, derived from the phenylpropanoid pathway
Carotenoids, derived from isoprenoid precursors
Betalains, derived from tyrosine
Chlorophyll derivatives
questions.correct_answer: Flavonoids, derived from the phenylpropanoid pathway
questions.explanation: Anthocyanins are glycosylated anthocyanidins, a subclass of flavonoids synthesized via the phenylpropanoid and flavonoid biosynthetic pathway starting from phenylalanine, distinguishing them from carotenoids and betalains.

questions.question: Alkaloids, a major class of nitrogen-containing plant secondary metabolites (e.g. caffeine, nicotine, morphine), are primarily derived biosynthetically from:
options: Amino acids such as lysine, tyrosine, and tryptophan
Fatty acids exclusively
The Calvin cycle intermediates directly
Cellulose degradation products
questions.correct_answer: Amino acids such as lysine, tyrosine, and tryptophan
questions.explanation: Most alkaloids are biosynthesized from amino acid precursors (e.g. tryptophan for indole alkaloids, tyrosine for isoquinoline alkaloids, lysine for piperidine alkaloids), often serving as chemical defenses against herbivores and pathogens.

questions.question: Terpenoids (isoprenoids), one of the largest classes of plant secondary metabolites, are all built from repeating units of:
options: Isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) and its isomer dimethylallyl pyrophosphate (DMAPP)
Acetyl-CoA condensed directly without intermediates
Glucose-1-phosphate
Malonyl-CoA exclusively
questions.correct_answer: Isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) and its isomer dimethylallyl pyrophosphate (DMAPP)
questions.explanation: Terpenoids are synthesized by head-to-tail or other condensations of the five-carbon building blocks IPP and DMAPP, produced via either the cytosolic mevalonate pathway or the plastidial MEP (methylerythritol phosphate) pathway.

questions.question: Phenylalanine ammonia-lyase (PAL), the entry-point enzyme of the phenylpropanoid pathway, catalyzes the conversion of phenylalanine to:
options: Cinnamic acid, by non-oxidative deamination
Tyrosine, by hydroxylation
Coumaric acid directly without intermediates
Salicylic acid
questions.correct_answer: Cinnamic acid, by non-oxidative deamination
questions.explanation: PAL removes an ammonia group from phenylalanine to form trans-cinnamic acid, the first committed step channeling primary metabolism (amino acid pool) into the phenylpropanoid pathway that produces lignin precursors, flavonoids, and other phenolics.

questions.question: Tannins, a class of polyphenolic secondary metabolites, contribute to plant defense mainly by:
options: Binding and precipitating proteins (including herbivore digestive enzymes), reducing digestibility and imparting an astringent taste
Acting as volatile signals for pollinator attraction
Directly poisoning herbivores via cyanide release
Serving as structural cell wall polysaccharides
questions.correct_answer: Binding and precipitating proteins (including herbivore digestive enzymes), reducing digestibility and imparting an astringent taste
questions.explanation: Tannins form complexes with dietary proteins and digestive enzymes in herbivores, reducing protein digestibility and nutrient availability, which deters feeding, while also often having antimicrobial properties.

questions.question: Auxin (indole-3-acetic acid, IAA) is synthesized in plants primarily via a pathway starting from:
options: Tryptophan
Methionine
Mevalonate
Phenylalanine
questions.correct_answer: Tryptophan
questions.explanation: The major auxin biosynthetic route in plants proceeds from the amino acid tryptophan via indole-3-pyruvate to indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), the principal naturally occurring auxin.

questions.question: The polar transport of auxin from shoot apex toward the root, essential for tropisms and apical dominance, depends on:
options: Asymmetric localization of PIN efflux carrier proteins on the basal end of cells
Passive diffusion alone with no carrier proteins
Xylem sap flow exclusively
Random Brownian motion between cells
questions.correct_answer: Asymmetric localization of PIN efflux carrier proteins on the basal end of cells
questions.explanation: PIN (PIN-FORMED) auxin efflux carriers are polarly localized to one end of each cell, creating a directional, cell-to-cell transport stream ('polar auxin transport') that establishes concentration gradients guiding tropic growth responses.

questions.question: Gibberellins promote seed germination in cereal grains by inducing the aleurone layer to synthesize:
options: Alpha-amylase, which hydrolyzes starch in the endosperm to provide sugars for the growing embryo
Chlorophyll for early photosynthesis
Cellulose for new cell walls only
Lignin to strengthen the seed coat
questions.correct_answer: Alpha-amylase, which hydrolyzes starch in the endosperm to provide sugars for the growing embryo
questions.explanation: Gibberellin released from the germinating embryo diffuses to the aleurone layer, triggering de novo synthesis and secretion of alpha-amylase and other hydrolases that mobilize stored starch in the endosperm to nourish the emerging seedling.

questions.question: Abscisic acid (ABA) plays a central role in plant water-stress responses primarily by:
options: Promoting stomatal closure via signaling that triggers efflux of K+ and anions from guard cells, reducing turgor
Directly increasing chlorophyll synthesis under drought
Stimulating cell elongation in roots under stress
Inhibiting seed dormancy
questions.correct_answer: Promoting stomatal closure via signaling that triggers efflux of K+ and anions from guard cells, reducing turgor
questions.explanation: Under water stress, ABA accumulates and binds receptors that activate signaling cascades (involving cytosolic Ca2+ and anion channel activation) in guard cells, causing loss of turgor and stomatal closure, reducing transpirational water loss.

questions.question: Ethylene biosynthesis in plants proceeds via the pathway: methionine to S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) to 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid (ACC) to ethylene. The enzyme ACC oxidase catalyzes:
options: The final step converting ACC to ethylene
The conversion of methionine to SAM
The conversion of SAM to ACC
Ethylene perception at the receptor
questions.correct_answer: The final step converting ACC to ethylene
questions.explanation: ACC synthase converts SAM to ACC (often the rate-limiting step), and ACC oxidase then catalyzes the final oxidative step releasing ethylene gas, along with CO2 and cyanide (detoxified via beta-cyanoalanine synthase).

questions.question: In response to pathogen attack, plants often mount a hypersensitive response (HR) involving localized cell death, which is closely associated with a rapid burst of:
options: Reactive oxygen species (ROS), such as superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, generated by NADPH oxidases
Increased chlorophyll synthesis at the infection site
Massive starch accumulation
Suppression of all defense gene expression
questions.correct_answer: Reactive oxygen species (ROS), such as superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, generated by NADPH oxidases
questions.explanation: The oxidative burst, driven by plasma membrane NADPH oxidases (RBOH proteins) and apoplastic peroxidases, generates ROS that contribute directly to pathogen killing, cell wall cross-linking, and signaling that reinforces localized programmed cell death (HR) to contain infection.

questions.question: Salicylic acid functions as a key plant signaling molecule that mediates:
options: Systemic acquired resistance (SAR) against biotrophic pathogens, partly by inducing pathogenesis-related (PR) protein expression
Stomatal closure during drought as the primary hormone
Fruit ripening as the principal signal
Cell elongation in the coleoptile
questions.correct_answer: Systemic acquired resistance (SAR) against biotrophic pathogens, partly by inducing pathogenesis-related (PR) protein expression
questions.explanation: Following localized infection, salicylic acid accumulates and signals (partly via the NPR1 protein) to activate PR gene expression both locally and systemically, priming distal tissues for enhanced resistance to subsequent pathogen attack (SAR).

questions.question: Phytoalexins are best described as:
options: Low-molecular-weight antimicrobial compounds synthesized de novo by plants in response to pathogen attack or stress
Constitutive structural compounds always present regardless of infection
Storage proteins found in seeds
Enzymes that degrade the pathogen's cell wall directly
questions.correct_answer: Low-molecular-weight antimicrobial compounds synthesized de novo by plants in response to pathogen attack or stress
questions.explanation: Unlike constitutive (preformed) defense compounds, phytoalexins (e.g. pisatin in peas, camalexin in Arabidopsis) are induced and synthesized only after infection or elicitor exposure, accumulating locally to inhibit pathogen growth.

questions.question: The plant vacuole, occupying a large proportion of mature cell volume, contributes to cellular biochemistry by all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Performing oxidative phosphorylation to generate ATP
Storing secondary metabolites, pigments (e.g. anthocyanins), and ions
Maintaining turgor pressure through osmotic water uptake
Serving as a lytic compartment analogous to the lysosome
questions.correct_answer: Performing oxidative phosphorylation to generate ATP
questions.explanation: Oxidative phosphorylation occurs in mitochondria, not the vacuole; the vacuole instead functions in storage (metabolites, pigments, ions), turgor maintenance, pH/ion homeostasis, and degradation of macromolecules via its hydrolytic enzymes.

questions.question: During seed germination, storage triglycerides in oil-rich seeds are converted to sucrose for transport to the growing embryo through a pathway that critically involves which specialized organelle performing the glyoxylate cycle?
options: Glyoxysomes
Chloroplasts
Golgi apparatus
Nucleolus
questions.correct_answer: Glyoxysomes
questions.explanation: Glyoxysomes, specialized peroxisome-like organelles in germinating oilseeds, house the glyoxylate cycle enzymes (isocitrate lyase and malate synthase) that allow net conversion of acetyl-CoA (from beta-oxidation of stored fats) into succinate, ultimately supporting gluconeogenesis to sucrose.

questions.question: The C4 photosynthetic decarboxylating enzyme NADP-malic enzyme, found in bundle sheath cells of many C4 plants (e.g. maize), catalyzes:
options: Oxidative decarboxylation of malate to pyruvate, CO2, and NADPH
Carboxylation of PEP to oxaloacetate
Reduction of oxaloacetate to malate
Phosphorylation of pyruvate to PEP
questions.correct_answer: Oxidative decarboxylation of malate to pyruvate, CO2, and NADPH
questions.explanation: In the NADP-malic enzyme subtype of C4 photosynthesis, malate transported into bundle sheath chloroplasts is oxidatively decarboxylated to release CO2 (for RuBisCO) and pyruvate, while generating NADPH usable in the Calvin cycle.
